title: What Is a Fever?
summary: What a fever is, how the brain raises body temperature to help fight germs, why we shiver and sweat, and how to care for someone with a fever.
poll: A fever is always a bad thing.

versions.title: Hot and Sick
versions.text:
Have you felt hot and sick? You may have had a fever. A fever is when you get too warm.

You are most often near 37 degrees. That is the heat it likes. With a fever, it gets to 38 or more.

Why does it get hot? Germs can make you sick. You fight them back. Your brain turns up the heat. Some germs do not like heat. They can not grow as fast.

A fever starts. You may feel cold. You shake. You shiver. That makes heat. Then the fever ends. You sweat. The sweat cools you.

Hot skin from the sun is not a fever. Play in the sun. You get hot. But you are not sick.

Do you have a fever? Use a thermometer. It shows how hot you are.

Rest in bed. Drink lots of water. You lose water when you sweat. Wear thin clothes. Only a grown-up should give you pills.

Some fevers need a doctor. Do you feel bad? Tell a grown-up. Does the fever last more than three days? Tell a grown-up.

versions.title: Hot and Sick
versions.text:
Have you felt hot and sick at once? You may have had a fever. A fever is when your body gets hotter than it should.

Most of the time, your body stays near 37 degrees. That is just right. When you have a fever, it goes up to 38 or more.

Germs can get into your body. They make you sick. Your body fights back. Your brain turns up your heat. It is like a heater in a room. Many germs do not like the heat. They can not grow as fast.

When a fever starts, you may feel cold. You shake and shiver. Shaking makes more heat. When the fever ends, you sweat. The sweat helps cool you down.

A fever is not the same as hot skin from the sun. Play outside in the summer, and you get hot. But you are not sick.

To check for a fever, use a thermometer. It shows how hot your body is.

If you have a fever, rest. Drink lots of water. You lose water when you sweat. Wear light clothes. Only a grown-up should give you medicine.

Some fevers need a doctor. Tell a grown-up if you feel very sick. Tell them if the fever lasts more than three days.

versions.title: What Is a Fever?
versions.text:
Have you ever felt hot, achy, and tired all at once? You may have had a fever. A fever happens when your body temperature rises above normal.

Most of the time, your body temperature stays close to 37 degrees Celsius. When you have a fever, your temperature rises to 38 degrees or higher.

A fever is not an illness by itself. It is a symptom, or a sign, that your body is fighting an infection. An infection happens when germs, such as viruses or bacteria, get inside your body and multiply. Your immune system is the part of your body that fights germs. When it finds them, it sends a message to your brain, and your brain turns up your body heat. Many germs cannot grow as quickly in a hot body.

When a fever begins, you may feel cold even though your body is warming up. You shiver, and shivering makes more heat. Later, when the fever breaks, you sweat. The sweat helps cool your body down.

A fever is different from feeling hot after playing in the summer sun. Your skin may feel warm outside, but you are not sick.

An adult can check for a fever with a thermometer, which measures your body temperature.

If you have a fever, rest and drink plenty of fluids, such as water, because you lose water when you sweat. Wear light clothes. Only an adult should give you medicine.

Some fevers need a doctor. Tell an adult if you feel very sick or if the fever lasts more than three days.

versions.title: Understanding Fever: The Body's Defense
versions.text:
Have you ever felt hot, achy, and tired all at the same time? If so, you probably had a fever, which occurs when your body temperature rises above its normal level.

A healthy body usually stays close to 37 degrees Celsius, and doctors generally consider a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or higher to be a fever.

A fever is not an illness by itself; instead, it is a symptom showing that your body is fighting an infection, which happens when germs such as viruses or bacteria get into your body and multiply. Your immune system finds these invaders and sends chemical messages to the hypothalamus, a small part of the brain that works like a thermostat in a house. The hypothalamus then raises the body's temperature setting, which helps because many germs cannot multiply as quickly in a warmer body, while the cells that fight germs work faster.

When a fever begins, you may feel cold even though your body is warming up, because your temperature is still below the new setting. You shiver, and the shaking muscles make extra heat. Later, when the fever breaks, the setting returns to normal, so you perspire, and the drying sweat cools your body down.

A fever is different from overheating after playing in the summer sun, since heat from outside does not change the brain's setting.

An adult can check for a fever with a thermometer, which measures body temperature; some thermometers go under the tongue or the arm, and others are held near the forehead or ear.

If you have a fever, rest and drink plenty of fluids, because sweating can cause dehydration, a dangerous loss of water. Wear light clothing, and remember that only an adult should give you medicine.

Most fevers from common colds last only two or three days. Still, some fevers need a doctor, so tell an adult if you feel very sick, have trouble breathing, or have a fever that lasts more than three days.

Have you ever felt hot, achy, and exhausted simultaneously? If so, you probably experienced a fever, which occurs when your body temperature rises noticeably above its normal level.

A healthy body usually remains close to 37 degrees Celsius, and physicians generally consider a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or higher to be a fever, although normal temperatures vary slightly from person to person and throughout the day.

A fever is not an illness by itself; instead, it is a symptom indicating that your body is combating an infection, which happens when microscopic germs such as viruses or bacteria enter your body and multiply. Your immune system detects these invaders and releases chemical messages that travel to the hypothalamus, a small region of the brain that functions like a thermostat in a house. The hypothalamus then raises the body's temperature setting, which is beneficial because many germs cannot multiply as rapidly in a warmer environment, while the specialized cells that fight germs operate considerably more efficiently.

When a fever begins, you may feel cold even though your body is warming up, because your temperature is still below the hypothalamus's new setting. Consequently, you shiver uncontrollably, and the vigorously shaking muscles generate additional heat. Later, when the fever breaks, the setting returns to normal, so you perspire, and the evaporating sweat gradually cools your body down.

A fever is different from overheating after playing in the summer sun, since heat absorbed from the surrounding environment does not alter the brain's internal temperature setting at all.

An adult can check for a fever with a thermometer, which measures body temperature accurately. Some thermometers are positioned under the tongue or the arm, while others are held near the forehead or gently inserted into the ear.

If you have a fever, rest and drink plenty of fluids, because continuous perspiration can cause dehydration, a potentially dangerous loss of water from the body, so wear lightweight, comfortable clothing, and remember that only a responsible adult should give you medicine.

versions.title: Understanding Fever: The Body's Defense
versions.text:
Have you ever felt simultaneously hot, achy, and thoroughly exhausted? If so, you have most likely experienced a fever, a condition that occurs whenever body temperature rises noticeably above its ordinary, healthy baseline. A typical healthy body remains close to 37 degrees Celsius, and physicians generally consider any reading of 38 degrees Celsius or higher to constitute a genuine fever, though normal baseline temperatures do vary somewhat from person to person and even across different times of day.

Importantly, a fever is not itself an illness; rather, it functions as a symptom indicating that the body is actively combating an underlying infection, which occurs whenever microscopic germs, such as viruses or bacteria, successfully enter the body and begin to multiply rapidly. The immune system detects these invading germs and promptly releases chemical signals that travel directly to the hypothalamus, a small but critically important region of the brain that functions remarkably similarly to a thermostat regulating temperature inside a house. Upon receiving this signal, the hypothalamus raises the body's internal temperature setting, a response that proves genuinely beneficial because many germs struggle to multiply as efficiently within a noticeably warmer internal environment, while the body's own specialized infection-fighting cells simultaneously operate considerably more efficiently at elevated temperatures.

As a fever first begins developing, a person may paradoxically feel cold even though their body is actively warming up, simply because their current temperature remains temporarily below the hypothalamus's newly elevated setting. This sensation triggers shivering, and the resulting muscular contractions generate additional heat to help close that gap. Later, once the underlying infection comes under control and the fever finally breaks, the hypothalamus's setting returns to its normal baseline, prompting the body to perspire, and this evaporating sweat gradually cools the body back down to its usual temperature.

A fever differs fundamentally from simply overheating after playing outdoors in the summer sun, since externally absorbed environmental heat never actually alters the hypothalamus's internal temperature setting the way a genuine infection does. An adult can reliably check for a fever using a thermometer, which accurately measures body temperature; some thermometers are positioned beneath the tongue or within the armpit, while others are held briefly near the forehead or gently inserted into the ear canal.

When experiencing a fever, resting adequately and drinking plenty of fluids proves essential, since continuous perspiration can otherwise lead to dehydration, a potentially dangerous loss of water from the body that develops surprisingly quickly if left unaddressed. Wearing lightweight, comfortable clothing helps as well, and only a responsible adult should ever administer medicine. Most fevers caused by common viruses resolve naturally within two or three days without any complications; nevertheless, certain fevers genuinely require professional medical attention, so any child should immediately tell a trusted adult if they feel extremely unwell, experience noticeable difficulty breathing, or find that their fever persists beyond three full days.

versions.title: Understanding Fever: The Body's Defense
versions.text:
Have you ever experienced the unsettling combination of feeling simultaneously hot, achy, and thoroughly exhausted all at once? If so, you have most likely experienced a fever, a physiological condition that occurs whenever a person's body temperature rises noticeably above its ordinary, healthy baseline level. A typical healthy human body remains close to 37 degrees Celsius under normal circumstances, and physicians generally consider any sustained reading of 38 degrees Celsius or higher to constitute a genuine clinical fever, although normal baseline temperatures do vary somewhat naturally from one individual to another and even across different hours of a single day.

Importantly, a fever does not itself constitute a distinct illness; rather, it functions as an observable symptom indicating that the body is actively engaged in combating some underlying infection, which occurs specifically whenever microscopic germs, such as viruses or bacteria, successfully penetrate the body's defenses and subsequently begin to multiply rapidly within its tissues. The immune system detects these invading germs almost immediately and promptly releases a cascade of chemical signals that travel directly toward the hypothalamus, a comparatively small yet critically important region of the brain that functions in a manner remarkably similar to a thermostat regulating ambient temperature inside an ordinary house. Upon receiving this urgent biochemical signal, the hypothalamus deliberately raises the body's internal temperature setting, a physiological response that proves genuinely beneficial precisely because many germs struggle considerably to multiply efficiently within a noticeably warmer internal environment, while the body's own specialized infection-fighting cells simultaneously operate with markedly greater efficiency under these elevated thermal conditions.

As a fever first begins to develop, an affected person may paradoxically feel distinctly cold even though their body is actively in the process of warming up, simply because their current measured temperature remains temporarily below the hypothalamus's newly and deliberately elevated setting. This uncomfortable sensation subsequently triggers involuntary shivering, and the resulting rapid muscular contractions generate meaningful additional heat specifically intended to help close that remaining thermal gap. Later, once the underlying infection comes fully under control and the fever ultimately breaks, the hypothalamus's internal setting promptly returns to its normal baseline level, prompting the body to perspire noticeably, and this gradually evaporating sweat steadily cools the body back down toward its usual, healthy resting temperature.

A fever differs fundamentally and importantly from simply overheating after playing outdoors beneath the summer sun, since externally absorbed environmental heat never actually alters the hypothalamus's carefully regulated internal temperature setting in the deliberate way that a genuine internal infection reliably does. A responsible adult can reliably check for a fever using an ordinary thermometer, which accurately measures body temperature with reasonable precision; some thermometers are positioned beneath the tongue or within the armpit, while others are instead held briefly near the forehead or gently inserted directly into the ear canal.

When experiencing a fever, resting adequately and drinking plentiful fluids throughout the day proves genuinely essential, since continuous, sustained perspiration can otherwise lead fairly quickly to dehydration, a potentially dangerous and sometimes serious loss of water from the body that can develop surprisingly rapidly if left entirely unaddressed. Wearing lightweight, comfortable clothing additionally helps considerably, and only a responsible, qualified adult should ever administer medicine under these circumstances. Most fevers caused by common, everyday viruses resolve naturally within approximately two or three days without any significant complications whatsoever; nevertheless, certain fevers genuinely require prompt professional medical attention, so any affected child should immediately inform a trusted adult if they feel extremely unwell, experience noticeable difficulty breathing, or find that their fever persists stubbornly beyond three full consecutive days.

keyWords.definition: when your body is hotter than normal, often because you are sick
keyWords.example: My little sister stayed home from school because she had a fever.

keyWords.definition: tiny living things that can make people sick
keyWords.example: We wash our hands with soap to get rid of germs.

keyWords.definition: a tool that measures how hot or cold something is
keyWords.example: The thermometer outside showed that it was very hot today.

keyWords.definition: to shake a little because you feel cold
keyWords.example: We began to shiver when we jumped into the cold pool.

keyWords.definition: to have water come out of your skin when you are hot
keyWords.example: Players sweat a lot during a football match.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to make your own thermometer at home
What a fever is and how to care for it
Why the summer sun feels so very hot
How people study to become doctors
questions.why: The article tells what a fever is, why it happens, and what to do when you have one.

wrong.A: A thermometer is used, but the article does not tell how to make one.
wrong.C: The sun is mentioned only to show it is not a fever.
wrong.D: The article does not tell how doctors are trained.

questions.stem: What is a normal body heat for most people?
options: About 30 degrees
About 45 degrees
About 37 degrees
About 50 degrees
questions.why: The article says the body is most often near 37 degrees.

wrong.A: 30 degrees is too low for a healthy body.
wrong.D: 50 degrees is not a body temperature in the article.

questions.stem: Why does the brain turn up the body's heat?
options: To make the skin look red and warm
Because the person ate far too much food
To help the body fall asleep faster
Because many germs grow slower in heat
questions.why: The article says many germs do not like heat and cannot grow as fast.

wrong.A: The article does not talk about red skin.
wrong.B: Eating too much is not given as a reason.
wrong.C: The article does not say heat helps you sleep.

questions.stem: What happens when a fever ends?
options: You sweat, and the sweat cools you.
You shiver more and more.
Your body gets hotter.
You need a thermometer to cool down.
questions.why: The article says that when the fever ends, you sweat, and the sweat cools you.

wrong.B: Shivering happens when the fever starts.
wrong.C: The body cools down when a fever ends.
wrong.D: A thermometer measures heat; it does not cool you.

questions.stem: In the article, the word "shiver" means —
options: to drink a glass of water
to shake because you feel cold
to sleep for a long, long time
to get a red sunburn outside
questions.why: The article says you may feel cold and shake and shiver, which makes heat.

wrong.A: Drinking water is a way to care for a fever.
wrong.D: A sunburn comes from the sun, not from shivering.

questions.stem: Why should you drink lots of water when you have a fever?
options: Water makes germs grow.
Water makes the fever hotter.
You lose water when you sweat.
Water is a kind of medicine pill.
questions.why: The article says to drink water because you lose water when you sweat.

wrong.A: The article does not say water helps germs.
wrong.B: Water does not make the fever hotter.
wrong.D: Water is not a pill.

questions.stem: Omar played football in the hot sun, and his skin feels hot. He feels fine. What does the article help us know?
options: Omar has a very bad fever.
Omar needs a doctor right away.
Omar should take a pill now.
Omar is hot, but not sick.
questions.why: The article says hot skin from the sun is not a fever, and you are not sick.

wrong.A: Hot skin from playing in the sun is not a fever.
wrong.B: He feels fine, so the article gives no reason for a doctor.
wrong.C: Only an adult should give medicine, and he is not sick.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article with when to tell a grown-up?
options: To keep readers safe if a fever is bad
To show that every single fever is dangerous
To tell readers that they never need a doctor
To explain how germs grow inside the body
questions.why: The ending tells readers the signs that mean they need more help.

wrong.B: The article says only some fevers need a doctor.
wrong.C: The ending says some fevers do need a doctor.
wrong.D: Germs are explained earlier, not at the end.

LOW.prompt: Your friend has a fever. Write three things your friend should do to feel better, and tell why.
checklist: I gave three ways to care for a fever.
I explained why one of them helps, like drinking water.
I said when to tell a grown-up.
LOW.modelAnswer: My friend with a fever should rest and drink plenty of water, because sweating makes the body lose water. My friend should also wear light clothes to feel more comfortable while shivering or sweating. If the fever lasts more than three days, my friend should tell a grown-up, because some fevers caused by germs need a doctor.

questions.why: Germs cause an infection, the fever begins with shivering, and sweating comes when it breaks.

questions.stem: How is a fever different from feeling hot after playing in the sun?

MID.prompt: Explain how a fever helps the body fight an infection. Use the words immune system and temperature.
checklist: I explained that germs cause an infection.
I described how the immune system and brain raise the temperature.
I explained why a higher temperature helps.
MID.modelAnswer: When germs get inside the body and cause an infection, the immune system finds them and sends a message to the brain. The brain then raises the body's temperature, which is why a fever happens. This higher temperature helps because many germs cannot grow as quickly in a hot body, so the fever actually helps the immune system fight off the infection.

keyWords.definition: a small part of the brain that controls body temperature, hunger, and thirst
keyWords.example: When you are thirsty, your hypothalamus helps tell you to drink.

keyWords.definition: a device that keeps a room or machine at a chosen temperature
keyWords.example: Dad set the thermostat so the air conditioner would keep the room cool.
Weeds multiply fast in a garden after the rain.

keyWords.definition: a harmful loss of too much water from the body
keyWords.example: Drinking water on hot days helps prevent dehydration.

keyWords.definition: a scale for measuring temperature, where water freezes at 0 and boils at 100

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the article?

A fever is the brain-guided way the body fights infection.

wrong.C: Heat from the sun does not change the brain's setting, so it is not a fever.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare the hypothalamus to a thermostat?

questions.stem: According to the article, why do you feel cold when a fever is starting?

wrong.D: A thermometer only measures temperature.

questions.stem: What happens to the hypothalamus's setting when a fever breaks?
options: It rises even higher than before.
It returns to normal, so you sweat.
It stops working completely for a day.
It moves to a different part of the body.

wrong.A: The setting goes down, not up, when a fever breaks.
wrong.C: It keeps working; it just returns to normal.

HIGH.prompt: Explain step by step what happens in the body from the moment germs enter until the fever breaks. Include the hypothalamus in your answer.
checklist: I explained how the immune system signals the hypothalamus.
I described why the body shivers and later sweats.
I included at least one way to care for a fever safely.
HIGH.modelAnswer: When germs enter the body and begin to multiply, the immune system detects them and sends a signal to the hypothalamus, the brain's thermostat that controls body temperature. The hypothalamus then raises the body's set temperature above the normal 37 degrees Celsius, and because the body thinks it should be hotter, a person shivers to generate more heat even though their temperature is already rising. Once the infection is under control and the fever breaks, the body sweats to cool back down, so it is important to drink plenty of fluids during this time to avoid dehydration.
